articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities in Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Actions
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This action underscores the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to disrupting illicit financial networks that support criminal and terrorist organizations globally.

These designations aim to sever financial lifelines and limit the ability of these groups to operate and fund their illicit activities. The specific individuals and entities added to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List were not detailed in the initial announcement but are part of broader efforts to safeguard the international financial system from abuse.
The action follows previous designations in October 2026 under similar authorities, indicating a sustained focus on these critical areas of national security.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Sanctions List, Modifies Entry for Volta Shipping Services LLC
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an Iran Designation Update on November 9, 2026, which included changes to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List. This update specifically modified the entry for Volta Shipping Services LLC.

The modification involved an alias change for Volta Shipping Services LLC, which is now also known as Volta Container Line FZCO. The entity's addresses and other identifying information in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, remain consistent.

This administrative update is part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to maintain the accuracy and effectiveness of its sanctions lists, ensuring that all relevant identifying information for sanctioned entities is current.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Eight Canadian Money Services Businesses for Facilitating Iranian Sanctions Evasion
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated eight Canada-based money services businesses (MSBs) on November 6, 2026, for operating in the digital asset sector of the Iranian economy. This action, part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' targets networks accused of helping Iran circumvent financial restrictions through cryptocurrency transactions and international currency transfers.

According to OFAC, these businesses exchanged Iranian rials and other currencies for digital assets, facilitating transactions with sanctioned Iranian digital asset exchanges and addresses associated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Several of the designated entities also allegedly sent or received funds from addresses linked to terrorism and laundered drug proceeds for a Canadian drug trafficker.

The sanctioned entities include Million Exchange, Amin Exchange, NIA Nations Currency Ltd., Farah Exchange, CCC Inc., Cryptoyal, Darvish Exchange, and Top PC Technician Inc., operating primarily in Ontario and British Columbia. This action follows earlier sanctions against Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges in June and August 2026, expanding the scope of 'Operation Economic Outcast' to include fiat-to-crypto intermediaries outside Iran.

articles.headline: OFAC Targets Global Scam Networks and Cuban Regime's Illicit Revenue
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations, alongside new Cuba designations. This action includes the publication of a Cuba-related determination pursuant to Executive Order 14404, focusing on the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of the Cuban economy.

The designations against transnational criminal organizations aim to disrupt global scam networks and the corporate infrastructure that enables them, including those facilitating cyber scams and money laundering. OFAC also targeted a Malaysian individual accused of managing a network of Africa-based scammers.

Regarding Cuba, OFAC added vessels and entities to the SDN List, such as the LPG Tanker EMILIA and Chemical/Products Tanker GLORIA C, both flagged to Cuba, and linked to entities involved in the Cuban economy. These measures are intended to further sanction the Cuban regime's foreign military support and illicit revenue networks.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran Shadow Fleet and Aviation Networks, Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, targeting individuals and entities linked to a network providing fraudulent vessel flags and maritime certifications to Iran's shadow fleet. This action, part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' also targeted a Türkiye-based company supporting sanctioned Iranian airlines.

Concurrently, OFAC issued an alert warning about sanctions risks associated with falsely flagged vessels used by Iran's shadow fleet, which are often involved in transporting Iranian petroleum. The State Department also designated individuals and an entity involved in procuring man-portable air-defense systems for Iran.

In addition to the Iran-related actions, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License 5AA, authorizing certain transactions involving the PDVSA 2020 8.5% bond on or after December 18, 2026, replacing General License 5Z. OFAC also amended FAQ 595 to reflect this updated authorization.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License for Wind Down of International Development Bank for Investment and Finance
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Iran General License FF-1 on October 29, 2026. This general license, titled 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance,' facilitates the orderly cessation of certain activities.

This amended general license provides a specific authorization for the wind-down of transactions, indicating a targeted approach to managing the impact of sanctions while allowing for a period of adjustment for affected parties.
Such general licenses are a common tool used by OFAC to mitigate unintended consequences of sanctions and provide clarity to the private sector regarding permissible activities.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Facilitators of DPRK IT Worker Fraud and Rwandan Ministry of Defence
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting individuals and entities related to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The North Korea-related actions target facilitators of DPRK IT worker fraud, including Russian and North Korean nationals linked to entities like LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY ALIS, CHINYONG INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY COOPERATION COMPANY, and FIRST FINANCIAL AND TECHNICAL DEVELOPMENT CENTER.

These designations aim to disrupt networks that generate revenue for North Korea's illicit weapons programs through the exploitation of IT workers. Several entries include listed digital wallets on Ethereum and TRON, highlighting the use of digital assets in these illicit schemes.

In relation to the DRC, OFAC sanctioned Rwanda's Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Kigali-based financial institution. These actions respond to Rwanda's alleged destabilizing activities in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and its support for the M23 rebel group.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a $1,529,685 settlement with Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, on October 27, 2026. The settlement resolves nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and related services to Joint Stock Company (JSC) Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA was majority-owned by the designated JSC Concern Almaz-Antey, making it a blocked person by operation of law, even though MMZA itself was not directly designated until June 2022.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious, citing reckless disregard for U.S. sanctions and substantial harm to U.S. foreign policy objectives. Extreme Networks also entered into a parallel non-prosecution agreement with the Department of Justice.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking and Rejecting Transactions and Filing Reports
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) amended several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, as part of its ongoing review of published guidance. This update focuses on the topics of Blocking and Rejecting Transactions and Filing Reports with OFAC.

The revised FAQs, including numbers 10, 32 through 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53, aim to ensure that information remains current and provides clarity on compliance obligations. Key areas addressed include when to block versus reject a transaction, the interest required on blocked funds, how to deduct service charges, and the timing and procedures for reporting blocked property and rejected transactions.

While these amendments do not introduce new sanctions programs or designations, they are significant for financial institutions and businesses as examiners, auditors, and OFAC's enforcement staff refer to these FAQs when assessing sanctions compliance.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran and Russia General Licenses, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced Iran-related designations, Belarus and North Korea designations removals, and the issuance of new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses on October 21, 2026. OFAC issued Iran General License GG, 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving Karnakis and Karnakis,' and Iran General License HH, 'Authorizing Wind Down Activities, Limited Safety and Environmental Transactions, and the Offloading of Cargo Involving Certain Persons or Vessels Blocked on October 21, 2026.'

Additionally, OFAC issued Russia-related General License 131K, 'Authorizing Certain Transactions for the Negotiation of and Entry Into Contingent Contracts for the Sale of Lukoil International GmbH and Related Maintenance Activities.' Two amended Frequently Asked Questions, FAQ 1224 and FAQ 1225, were also released.

The action also included updates to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List, with new individuals and entities added under Iran-related authorities, and certain individuals and entities removed from the SDN list under Belarus and North Korea sanctions programs.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Pays $1.5 Million OFAC Penalty for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle its potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations. The settlement was announced by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 27, 2026.

The violations stemmed from Extreme Networks' export of networking equipment and related services to Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer, between September 2018 and March 2022. MMZA was majority-owned by a designated entity, JSC Concern Almaz-Antey, making it a blocked person under OFAC's 50 Percent Rule.

OFAC determined that the violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious, highlighting the importance of thorough due diligence, especially when acquiring customer contracts and overseeing foreign affiliates. The company also entered into a parallel non-prosecution agreement with the Department of Justice.

Details of the specific violations leading to this penalty were not immediately released in the summary, but such large fines typically involve multiple transactions or systemic failures in sanctions screening and compliance. Financial institutions are expected to implement comprehensive controls to prevent transactions with sanctioned entities or individuals.
This enforcement action serves as a reminder to all financial institutions of the severe consequences of failing to adhere to U.S. sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: BIS Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List. This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with those already applied to firearms.

Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and BIS will require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers of these newly controlled items, including related software and technology. License exceptions currently available for firearms will also be applicable to suppressors.

This change is intended to alleviate compliance burdens on the firearms industry while continuing to protect national security. The BIS and Department of State Federal Register notices implementing these regulatory changes are available online for further details.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
